Adrenal: Total cortisol rises; free cortisol is unchanged; aldosterone rises (salt and water retention)
Renal excretion (principal cells of cortical collecting duct) is modulated by aldosterone, distal flow, and acid‑base status.

The fall in intravascular volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH, so the kidney retains salt and water, and some primary sodium retention at the distal nephron (overfill) adds to the swelling.

qs.q: Secretion of aldosterone would be affected if which layer of the adrenal cortex is damaged? ---
o: Fasciculata makes cortisol; reticularis makes sex steroids.
qs.e: Aldosterone is synthesized by cells of the zona glomerulosa. Damage to this outer cortical layer therefore directly reduces aldosterone production.

qs.q: Stimulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) by the kidney primarily occurs in response to ---
o: Decreased sodium delivery to the distal tubule
Decreased potassium levels in extracellular fluid
qs.e: Only a small fraction of filtered water is ultimately excreted as urine; most filtered water is reabsorbed along the nephron. The exact fraction varies with physiological conditions.

qs.q: Aldosterone primarily acts on which part of the nephron to increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion?
o: Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
qs.e: Aldosterone, a mineralocorticoid, primarily acts on the principal cells in the late distal convoluted tubule and cortical collecting duct. It stimulates the insertion of more ENaC channels (for Na+ reabsorption) and ROMK channels (for K+ secretion) into the apical membrane, and Na+/K+-ATPase pumps into the basolateral membrane, leading to increased Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion. ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Aldosterone is the kidney's key hormone for sodium retention and potassium excretion, controlling blood volume and pressure. It acts on the distal nephron via the mineralocorticoid receptor. Clinicians use its level to diagnose disorders of fluid balance.

sections.p: Aldosterone is produced in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. It is the principal mineralocorticoid, linking the renin‑angiotensin system to sodium and water homeostasis.
b: Stimulated by angiotensin II, high K⁺, and ACTH
Acts on principal cells of the cortical collecting duct

sections.p: Aldosterone binds the intracellular mineralocorticoid receptor, translocates to the nucleus and up‑regulates ENaC and Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase, increasing Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion.
b: Na⁺ reabsorption creates an osmotic gradient that pulls water into the intravascular space
K⁺ loss can cause hypokalaemia, muscle weakness, arrhythmias

sections.p: The renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system (RAAS) is the dominant feedback loop: low renal perfusion → renin → angiotensin I → angiotensin II → aldosterone. High plasma K⁺ directly stimulates zona glomerulosa cells.
b: Renin release is inhibited by increased Na⁺ delivery to the macula densa
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and direct renin inhibitors blunt aldosterone production

sections.p: Abnormal aldosterone production disrupts fluid balance, leading to hypertension, hypokalaemia, or volume depletion.
b: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) – autonomous secretion, low renin
Secondary hyperaldosteronism – excess renin from heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, or renal artery stenosis
Aldosterone deficiency – adrenal insufficiency, bilateral adrenalectomy

sections.p: Measuring aldosterone and renin helps differentiate causes of hypertension and electrolyte disturbances, guiding targeted therapy.

t.b: Screen for primary hyperaldosteronism; a high ratio (>20) with elevated aldosterone suggests autonomous secretion
Detect hypokalaemia from excess aldosterone; low K⁺ supports diagnosis
Distinguish primary (low PRA) from secondary (high PRA) hyperaldosteronism

sections.p: Focus on the physiology‑pathology link, the ARR interpretation, and the first‑line drugs for excess aldosterone.
b: Conn syndrome: hypertension, hypokalaemia, suppressed renin, high aldosterone
Spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor; used in primary hyperaldosteronism and heart failure
In low‑resource settings, a simple ARR can be done with bedside renin kits and serum aldosterone ELISA

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertension (>180/120 mmHg) with neurological symptoms
Profound hypokalaemia (<2.5 mmol/L) causing muscle paralysis or arrhythmia
Acute adrenal crisis with hypotension and hyperkalaemia

faq.a: It increases sodium reabsorption, expanding extracellular volume and raising arterial pressure.

faq.q: Can low aldosterone cause low blood pressure?
faq.a: Yes; insufficient sodium retention leads to volume depletion and hypotension, seen in adrenal insufficiency.

faq.q: What is the first test for suspected primary hyperaldosteronism?
faq.a: Measure the aldosterone‑to‑renin ratio; a high ratio prompts confirmatory testing.

exam: Explain how aldosterone regulates potassium and why hypokalaemia occurs in primary hyperaldosteronism.
Interpret an aldosterone‑to‑renin ratio of 30 with aldosterone 70 ng/dL and renin 0.2 ng/mL/hr.
List the pharmacologic actions of spironolactone and why it is preferred over thiazides in hyperaldosteronism.
